## Overview

## 1. Hydrologic Context and Systemic Stress

The Colorado River Basin entered its 27th consecutive year of drought in 2026 under conditions that constitute the most severe hydrological regime in the instrumental record. Lake Powell and Lake Mead—the system's two largest reservoirs—stand at 25% and 29% of capacity, respectively, yielding an aggregate system storage of approximately 34% of designed capacity [6][2]. The 2026 water year produced one of the lowest April–July inflow volumes on record into Lake Powell: 800,000 acre-feet (AF), equivalent to 15% of the normal forecast, a deficit amplified by the lowest snowpack on record and record-breaking March–April heat [6]. This shortfall can be expressed as a volumetric deficit relative to the 30-year normal:

$$\Delta Q_{\text{inflow}} = Q_{\text{normal}} - Q_{2026} = Q_{\text{normal}} - 0.15\,Q_{\text{normal}} = 0.85\,Q_{\text{normal}}$$

With a typical April–July inflow near 5.3 MAF, the implied deficit is on the order of 4.5 MAF—exceeding the entire annual consumptive use of Nevada. The resulting operational stress on the Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) is acute: reservoir elevations must remain above critical thresholds to sustain hydropower generation at Glen Canyon and Hoover Dams, yet the 2026 inflow trajectory leaves minimal regulatory headroom [6][2]. Reclamation's 24-Month Study, the operational instrument that translates hydrologic projections into release decisions, consequently drives every allocation and shortage trigger discussed below [9].
